section.title: Theme E: Religion, crime and punishment
section.blurb: Good and evil, reasons for crime, attitudes to lawbreakers, aims of punishment, treatment of criminals, forgiveness and the death penalty.

topics.title: Crime, good and evil intentions and actions
topics.overview: Know what a crime is, how religious and non-religious people judge good and evil intentions and actions, and why they think intentions matter. The question of whether it can ever be good to cause suffering is covered in its own topic.

bullets: A **crime** is an offence which is punishable by law, for example stealing or murder. Crimes can be against a person (murder, assault), against property (theft, vandalism) or against the state (terrorism, treason).

A **law** is a rule that a country makes and everyone must keep. A **religious moral law** is a rule from God or a religion, such as the Ten Commandments ('You shall not steal', 'You shall not murder').

Some actions are crimes and also sins (murder, theft). Some are sins for many believers but not crimes (lying in most situations, adultery). Some good actions are not required by law (giving to charity).

In the UK, someone found guilty by a court can be fined, given a community sentence or sent to prison. Murder carries a mandatory life sentence. The UK does not use the death penalty or corporal punishment.

notes.h: Good and evil intentions and actions
bullets: **Good** means morally right or beneficial; **evil** means extremely wicked and immoral, causing harm or suffering.

An **intention** is what a person means or plans to do. The same action can be judged differently depending on intention: killing someone deliberately (murder) is treated far more seriously than killing someone by accident (manslaughter). UK law also asks whether a person had a 'guilty mind'.

Christians believe intentions matter as well as actions. Jesus taught that anger and lust in the heart are already sinful (Matthew 5:21-22, 5:28), and that 'from within, out of the hearts of men, proceed evil thoughts... murders, thefts' (Mark 7:21). God judges the heart.

Christians believe humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27) but affected by **original sin**, so everyone is capable of evil: 'all have sinned' (Romans 3:23). Paul admitted, 'the evil which I don't desire, that I practise' (Romans 7:19). So Christians say 'hate the sin, love the sinner'.
Many Christians also link evil to temptation by Satan (the devil), though they say people are still responsible for their choices because God gave free will.

Jews do not believe in original sin. Every person has a **yetzer hatov** (inclination to do good) and a **yetzer hara** (inclination to do evil), and has free will to choose. Ecclesiastes 7:20 says no one is so good that they never do wrong.

In Judaism actions matter most, but intention (**kavanah**) also counts. When Rabbi Meir prayed for some troublemakers to die, his wife Beruriah told him to pray that their sins would end, not the sinners (Talmud, Berakhot 10a).

Humanists judge actions by their effects on human well-being and by reason and empathy, not by God's commands. Most accept that intentions matter: a person who meant well but caused harm is judged differently from one who meant harm.
A **utilitarian** judges an action mainly by its consequences: does it bring the greatest good for the greatest number? On this view a good intention does not make a harmful action right.
The philosopher Immanuel Kant argued the opposite: what matters most is acting from a good will and doing your duty, whatever the consequences.

Many non-religious people (and religious ones) argue that social causes, such as poverty, poor education or abuse, help explain why people commit crime, though people are still responsible for what they do.

views.label: Christian
views.text: Intentions matter as well as actions, because Jesus said evil starts in the heart. All humans can do evil because of original sin, but God offers forgiveness, so believers hate the sin but love the sinner.

views.label: Jewish
views.text: There is no original sin. Each person has a good and an evil inclination and the free will to choose between them. Actions matter greatly, and repentance (teshuvah) is always possible.

views.label: Utilitarian
views.text: An action is good or evil because of its consequences, the amount of happiness or suffering it produces, rather than because of the intention behind it.

views.label: Humanist
views.text: Morality comes from reason and empathy, not God. Intentions and consequences both matter, and society should tackle the social causes that lead people to do harm.

topics.title: Reasons for crime and views about people who break the law
topics.overview: AQA lists poverty and upbringing, mental health problems and addiction, greed and hate, and opposition to an unjust law as reasons for crime. For each, know how it can lead to crime and what religious and non-religious people think about people who break the law for that reason.

bullets: **Poverty** means being without money, food or other basic needs. Some people steal to survive or are drawn into crime such as drug dealing to earn money.

**Upbringing** is the way a child is raised and the environment they grow up in. Children who experience neglect, abuse or family members involved in crime may copy what they see or never learn right from wrong.

Religious views: theft is still wrong, but it can be understandable. 'Men don't despise a thief, if he steals to satisfy himself when he is hungry' (Proverbs 6:30), though the verse goes on to say he must still repay. Christians and Jews believe society has a duty to help the poor so people do not need to steal: Jews give **tzedakah**, and churches and synagogues run food banks (for example through the Trussell network). Christians stress good parenting (Ephesians 6:4), and Judaism teaches parents to bring up children in the mitzvot.
Some **mental health problems** can affect judgement or self-control, and in rare cases lead to crime. A court may decide a person needs treatment in a secure hospital rather than prison.

**Addiction** is a physical or mental dependency on a substance or activity, such as drugs, alcohol or gambling. People may steal to pay for their addiction, or commit crimes while under the influence.

Religious views: believers should show compassion and support recovery, because every person is made in God's image. Christians see drunkenness as wrong (Ephesians 5:18) but many churches run addiction support. Jews see the body as a gift from God that must be looked after. Both say offenders still have some responsibility and need help to change.

**Greed** is the selfish desire for more than you need, for example money, possessions or power. It can lead to theft, fraud or robbery. 'The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil' (1 Timothy 6:10); the Ten Commandments forbid coveting (Exodus 20:17).
**Hate** is intense dislike of someone. It can lead to violence, and to **hate crimes** targeting people because of race, religion, sexual orientation, disability or gender identity.

Religious views: greed and hate are condemned because they put self before God and neighbour. Most believers say these are the hardest reasons to sympathise with, because the crime is usually chosen and planned rather than forced by need.

An **unjust law** is a law that is unfair, for example because it discriminates or denies human rights. Some people break such laws as a protest (**civil disobedience**), usually openly and peacefully, accepting the punishment.

Examples: Rosa Parks, a Christian, refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1955; Martin Luther King broke segregation laws peacefully and was jailed. In the Bible the Hebrew midwives disobeyed Pharaoh's order to kill baby boys (Exodus 1:17), and Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refused to worship the king's statue (Daniel 3:18).

Christian teaching: obey the authorities because God allows them (Romans 13:1), but 'We must obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29) when a law is against God's law. Jesus said, 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's' (Mark 12:17).

Jewish teaching: 'the law of the land is the law' (dina d'malchuta dina), so Jews obey the law of the country they live in, except where it requires them to break God's commandments. The Talmud teaches that anyone who could protest against wrongdoing and does not shares responsibility for it (Shabbat 54b).
Most religious people say breaking an unjust law should be non-violent, a last resort, and done openly with willingness to accept the consequences.

notes.h: Views about people who break the law for these reasons
bullets: Christians condemn the crime but not the person: 'Don't judge, so that you won't be judged' (Matthew 7:1). They often feel more sympathy for crime caused by poverty, mental illness or addiction than by greed or hate, but still believe in justice.

Jews are taught, 'Do not judge your fellow until you have reached his place' (Pirkei Avot 2:4): consider a person's situation before condemning them. But offenders must still make restitution and do teshuvah.

Non-religious views: many humanists and criminologists argue that tackling poverty, poor education, mental illness and addiction prevents more crime than harsh punishment does. Others stress personal responsibility: many poor people never commit crime.
In UK courts, reasons can affect the sentence: mental illness or addiction may lead to treatment orders, while hate is an aggravating factor that makes a sentence harsher.

views.label: Christian
views.text: Some people are driven to crime by poverty, illness or addiction, so society should help them and offenders should be treated with compassion. People still have free will and must face the consequences, while being offered forgiveness.

views.label: Jewish
views.text: Communities must prevent crime through tzedakah, education and strong families. Do not judge someone until you have stood in their place, but criminals are responsible and must make restitution and repent.

views.label: Non-religious
views.text: Social causes such as poverty, poor upbringing and lack of opportunity explain much crime. Punishment alone does not work unless the causes are tackled, though individuals remain responsible for their choices.

topics.title: Types of crime: hate crime, theft and murder
topics.overview: AQA asks for views about different types of crime, including hate crimes, theft and murder. Know why religious and non-religious people see each as wrong, how the UK law deals with them, and recent examples and statistics.

bullets: A **hate crime** is a crime, often violent, motivated by hostility towards someone because of their race, religion, sexual orientation, disability or transgender identity. It can include assault, harassment, criminal damage and abuse online.

In England and Wales police recorded 146,825 hate crimes in the year to March 2026, up 7% on the year before. Religious hate crimes rose 13% to 11,419, the highest on record; Jews were by far the most targeted group relative to the size of their community (3,162 antisemitic offences, a rate about nine times that for Muslims). Source: Home Office figures published October 2026.
In UK law hostility is an aggravating factor, so courts give longer sentences.

Christian views: hate crime is wrong because all people are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27) and 'you are all one in Christ Jesus' (Galatians 3:28). 'If a man says, "I love God," and hates his brother, he is a liar' (1 John 4:20). The parable of the Good Samaritan shows love across religious and ethnic divides.

Example of a Christian response: in 2005 Anthony Walker, a Black teenager, was murdered in a racist attack in Liverpool. His mother, Gee Walker, a Christian, said publicly that she forgave the killers, and the Anthony Walker Foundation works against racism.

Jewish views: every person is made in God's image; the Torah commands love of the stranger (Leviticus 19:34). Jews have experienced centuries of hate crime, including the Holocaust and recent attacks such as at Heaton Park synagogue in 2025, so many Jewish organisations (for example the Community Security Trust) work against all hate crime.
Non-religious views: hate crime attacks human dignity and equality, which humanists defend for everyone.
**Theft** is stealing, taking something that belongs to someone else without permission. It is the most common type of crime against property.
Religious views: 'You shall not steal' (Exodus 20:15). Theft breaks trust and harms victims. Some theft is driven by need, which believers find understandable, but they still say it is wrong.

Jewish law requires **restitution**: a thief must repay, and in some cases pay back double or more (Exodus 22:1 to 4). Zacchaeus, a tax collector who had cheated people, promised Jesus to pay back four times as much (Luke 19:8).

**Murder** is the unlawful, deliberate killing of another person. In the UK it carries a mandatory life sentence; for the very worst murders a judge can give a **whole life order**, meaning the person will never be released.

Religious views: murder is seen as the worst crime because it destroys a life made in God's image and breaks 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13). Only God should give and take life (sanctity of life). Judaism teaches that destroying one life is like destroying a whole world (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5). Jesus went further, saying even anger can be sinful (Matthew 5:21-22).
Even so, Christians and Jews believe a murderer can repent and be forgiven by God, though they still face punishment.

notes.h: How believers treat people who commit crimes
bullets: Christians separate the crime from the person: 'hate the sin, love the sinner'. Jesus said, 'I was in prison, and you came to me' (Matthew 25:36), so Christians visit prisoners and support them on release.

Christian organisations: Prison Fellowship runs the Sycamore Tree victim awareness course in prisons; Street Pastors patrol town centres at night to help keep people safe; prison chaplains of many faiths, including Jewish chaplains, visit prisoners.
Jews believe lawbreakers must be held accountable and make restitution, but can be forgiven if they do teshuvah.
Both traditions accept that laws are needed for order, and that offenders still have rights and deserve fair treatment.

views.label: Christian
views.text: Crime is condemned but the criminal is still loved by God, so believers hate the sin but love the sinner, visit prisoners and hope offenders will repent and change.

views.label: Jewish
views.text: Lawbreakers must be held accountable and make restitution to those they have harmed. Repentance (teshuvah) gives a fresh start, and hatred of any person made in God's image is forbidden.

views.label: Non-religious
views.text: Supports fair trials, equal protection for every group and rehabilitation. Some stress protecting society, while others focus on tackling the causes of crime.

Avoid stereotypes about how other religions punish crime. Show the range of views within each religion.

topics.title: The aims of punishment: retribution, deterrence and reformation
topics.overview: The three AQA aims are retribution, deterrence and reformation. Know what each means, its strengths and weaknesses, and what Christians, Jews and non-religious people (including utilitarians) think about each.

bullets: **Punishment** is something legally done to somebody as a result of being found guilty of breaking the law.

Most people agree punishment is needed: to show that crime is wrong, to protect the public, to give victims justice and to keep order. Religious believers add that God is just, and that justice is part of a fair society (Amos 5:24, Deuteronomy 16:20).

**Retribution**: an aim of punishment meaning 'getting your own back': the offender should suffer in proportion to the harm done. Strength: it feels fair and satisfies victims. Weakness: it can become revenge and does nothing to change the offender.

**Deterrence**: an aim of punishment intended to put people off committing crimes, both the offender (individual deterrence) and others (general deterrence). Strength: it may prevent future victims. Weakness: many crimes are committed on impulse or under the influence, without thinking of punishment.

**Reformation**: an aim of punishment which seeks to change a criminal's behaviour for the better, through education, therapy, training or restorative justice. Strength: if it works, there are fewer future victims. Weakness: victims may see it as too soft, and not every offender wants to change.
Other aims: **protection** of the public (for example keeping dangerous people in prison) and **reparation** (the offender making amends to the victim or community).
**Restorative justice** brings victims and offenders together, with their agreement, so the offender understands the harm done and can make amends. Many Christians, including the Quakers, support it.

Most Christians see **reformation** as the most important aim, because Jesus came to call sinners to repentance, taught forgiveness and gave people second chances (the woman caught in adultery, John 8:7-11; the penitent thief, Luke 23:42-43). God says 'I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live' (Ezekiel 33:11).
Christians accept that punishment is right and that the state has authority to punish wrongdoers (Romans 13:4). Many accept deterrence and protection.

Christians are wary of retribution because Jesus replaced 'eye for eye' with 'turn the other cheek' (Matthew 5:38-39) and Paul said 'Don't seek revenge yourselves' (Romans 12:19). Some Christians still argue that a fair, proportionate punishment is a form of justice, not revenge.
Judaism teaches that justice must be done: 'Justice, justice you shall pursue' (Deuteronomy 16:20). Punishment shows that God's law matters.

'Eye for eye, tooth for tooth' (Exodus 21:24) set a limit: punishment must fit the crime and no more. The rabbis taught it meant paying **financial compensation**, not physically injuring the offender (Talmud, Bava Kamma 84a).
Judaism also stresses restitution and teshuvah (repentance), so reformation matters too. Some Torah punishments were meant to deter: 'all the people shall hear, and fear' (Deuteronomy 17:13).

A **utilitarian** (following Jeremy Bentham) supports punishment only if it produces more good than harm overall, so deterrence, protection and reformation matter more than retribution for its own sake.
Others, following Kant, argue that offenders deserve punishment because they chose to do wrong, which supports retribution.

Many humanists support evidence-based policies that reduce reoffending: in recent years more than half of adults released from prison sentences of under 12 months in England and Wales reoffended within a year, which is one reason the Sentencing Act 2026 created a presumption that short sentences are suspended and served in the community.

views.label: Christian
views.text: Reformation should usually be the main aim because Jesus taught forgiveness and second chances and God wants the wicked to turn and live. Justice and protection matter too, but punishment must not become revenge.

views.label: Jewish
views.text: Justice must be done and punishment must fit the crime, but 'eye for eye' was understood as fair compensation. Restitution and repentance (teshuvah) are central so the offender can return to the community.

views.label: Utilitarian
views.text: Punishment is only justified by its results: deterring crime, protecting the public and reforming offenders so that the greatest number are better off. Suffering for its own sake is pointless.

views.label: Kantian
views.text: Offenders deserve to be punished because they freely chose to do wrong; justice requires that the punishment matches the crime, whatever the consequences.

topics.title: Can it ever be good to cause suffering?
topics.overview: The AQA specification asks whether it can ever be good to cause suffering. Know religious and non-religious arguments on both sides, with examples such as punishment, self-defence, medical treatment and discipline.

bullets: **Suffering** is pain, distress or hardship. **Natural suffering** comes from disease and disasters; **moral suffering** is caused by human choices, such as crime.

Christians believe God gave humans free will, which means people can choose to cause suffering. Christians try to reduce suffering, following Jesus, who healed the sick and suffered himself on the cross.

Christians can find meaning in suffering: 'suffering produces perseverance; and perseverance, proven character; and proven character, hope' (Romans 5:3-4). Discipline 'seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness' (Hebrews 12:11).
Jews may see suffering as a test, as in the story of Job, and stress faith and helping others. They are taught to repair the world (**tikkun olam**).

notes.h: Arguments that causing suffering is wrong
bullets: Christians and Jews say deliberately causing suffering is wrong because of love of neighbour (Leviticus 19:18, Matthew 22:39), the sanctity of life and 'You shall not murder'.
Jesus taught 'Repay no one evil for evil' (Romans 12:17) and showed compassion to sinners, so causing suffering as revenge is wrong.
Judaism forbids causing needless suffering even to animals (**tza'ar ba'alei chayim**), so causing it to people is even more serious.

Humanists argue that because this life is the only one, causing suffering takes away the only happiness people have. The **harm principle** of J. S. Mill says people should be free to act as they wish unless they harm others.

notes.h: Arguments that causing suffering can sometimes be right
bullets: **Punishment**: fair punishment causes hardship (loss of freedom, a fine), but most believers accept it is right for justice, protection and reform. The state 'doesn't bear the sword in vain' (Romans 13:4).
**Self-defence and protecting others**: using force against an attacker causes suffering but can save innocent lives (Exodus 22:2; just war theory).
**Medical treatment**: a doctor causes pain (surgery, chemotherapy) to heal. The intention is good and the suffering is proportionate.
**Discipline and tough love**: parents and teachers sometimes cause short-term unhappiness (a sanction) for long-term good (Hebrews 12:11).
Religious believers stress that in all these cases the intention must be good, the suffering must be proportionate, and it must never be the aim in itself.

A **utilitarian** accepts causing suffering if it prevents greater suffering, for example punishing one person to deter many. Critics say this could justify punishing an innocent person to calm a crowd, which most people think is clearly wrong.

Some believers point out that God can bring good from suffering, as with Joseph: 'you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good' (Genesis 50:20). This does not make it right to cause the suffering.

notes.h: Responding to suffering caused by crime
bullets: After the 2015 Charleston church shooting in the USA, relatives of some of the nine victims publicly forgave the killer.
Restorative justice lets victims explain the suffering caused, which can help offenders understand and change.

views.label: Christian
views.text: Believers should reduce suffering and never cause it for its own sake. Fair punishment, self-defence or medical treatment may cause hardship for a good purpose, but they must be proportionate and come from love, not revenge.

views.label: Jewish
views.text: Causing needless suffering, even to animals, breaks the Torah, and harm must be repaired. Defence of life or just punishment can justify limited suffering, always with the aim of protecting life.

views.label: Utilitarian
views.text: Causing suffering is right only if it leads to less suffering overall, for example deterring crime or protecting many people. The consequences decide.

views.label: Humanist
views.text: Causing suffering is wrong because this life is the only one, unless it is needed to prevent greater harm to others. People should be free to act unless they harm others.

pitfalls: Do not just write about why God allows suffering. The spec issue is whether humans can ever be right to cause it.
Always give a condition: good intention, proportionate, and a greater good. Without these, causing suffering is condemned by all the traditions.
Do not say a utilitarian 'likes suffering'. They accept it only if it reduces suffering overall.

topics.title: The treatment of criminals: prison, corporal punishment and community service
topics.overview: Know the three forms of treatment AQA names, with Christian, Jewish and non-religious views on each. Corporal punishment is one of AQA's three 'contrasting beliefs' issues, so learn clearly contrasting views on it.

bullets: **Prison** is a secure building where offenders are held for a period of time as punishment. It aims to protect the public, punish (retribution), deter and reform through education, training and drug treatment.

UK context (2025 to 2026): prisons in England and Wales held around 87,000 to 88,000 people, close to full capacity. This led to early release schemes from 2024 and the **Sentencing Act 2026**, which (from March 2026) presumes that sentences of 12 months or less are suspended and served in the community, and (from October 2026) lets many prisoners be released after a third of their sentence.
Criticisms: overcrowding, violence and drugs in prisons; high reoffending; prison can be a 'school for crime'. Supporters say it is the only way to protect the public from dangerous offenders.

Christian views: Christians accept prison for serious crimes but want it to be humane and reforming. Jesus said 'I was in prison, and you came to me' (Matthew 25:36) and Hebrews 13:3 says 'Remember those who are in bonds'. Elizabeth Fry, a Quaker, reformed conditions for women prisoners in the 1800s. Today prison chaplains and Prison Fellowship support prisoners.

Jewish views: the Torah mostly uses restitution rather than prison, but Jews today accept prison for serious crime. Jewish chaplains visit Jewish prisoners, and Judaism stresses teshuvah and returning to the community.
**Corporal punishment** is punishing an offender by causing them physical pain, for example caning, whipping or flogging.

UK law: courts stopped using corporal punishment in 1948. It was banned in state schools in 1987 and in all schools by 2003. Parents' smacking has been banned in Scotland (2020) and Wales (2022). As of 2026, parents in England can still use the defence of 'reasonable punishment' for mild smacking, despite campaigns (including by Humanists UK and children's charities) to remove it. Some countries, such as Singapore, still use judicial caning.

**Christians against**: most denominations oppose it. It goes against human dignity (made in God's image), Jesus' teaching to love and not repay evil for evil, and the aim of reformation. Violence can breed violence: 'all those who take the sword will die by the sword' (Matthew 26:52). Many Christians support ending physical punishment of children.

**Christians for**: a minority, often from more conservative traditions, point to 'One who spares the rod hates his son' (Proverbs 13:24) and argue that mild physical discipline by loving parents can be right. Some Christian groups, such as the Christian Institute, have argued against smacking bans.

**Jewish views**: the Torah allowed flogging with a strict limit of forty lashes so the offender would not be humiliated (Deuteronomy 25:2-3), and the rabbis made it rarer still. It is not used by Jewish courts today, and most Jews oppose it, reading 'the rod' in Proverbs as guidance and discipline rather than hitting.

**Non-religious views**: most humanists oppose it as cruel, degrading and ineffective; research links physical punishment of children with worse behaviour. Some argue (using the principle of utility) that a quick physical punishment is cheaper than prison and might deter others.

**Community service** is a punishment, also called unpaid work or Community Payback, for minor crimes. Offenders do between 40 and 300 hours of unpaid work, such as clearing litter, removing graffiti or decorating community centres, while living at home.
It is used for less serious crimes, not for murder or serious violence.

Supporters say it reforms offenders, repays the community (reparation), avoids the bad influence of prison and costs less. Critics say it can seem too soft and some offenders do not complete their hours.
Christians and Jews generally support it because it allows reformation and making amends. Jews link it to tikkun olam (repairing the world) and teshuvah.

views.label: Most Christians
views.text: Prison and community service are acceptable when they protect people and help offenders change, but physical punishment harms human dignity and goes against Jesus' teaching of love, so it should not be used.

views.label: Conservative minority
views.text: Mild physical discipline of children by loving parents can be right because scripture says that whoever spares the rod hates his son, and bans on smacking interfere with parents' rights.

views.label: Jewish
views.text: Justice and repair matter most. Prison is accepted for serious crimes and community service fits tikkun olam. The Torah limited flogging to forty lashes, but it is not used today and most oppose physical punishment.

views.label: Humanist
views.text: Physical punishment is cruel and degrading and the evidence shows it does not work; punishments should be humane and judged by whether they reduce reoffending.

pitfalls: Examiners gave no marks when answers on corporal punishment wrote about capital punishment instead. Corporal means physical pain; capital means death.
Community service is for minor crimes. Do not argue it is unsuitable because murderers would get it; they would not.
Do not say Christians reject prison completely. Examiners did not credit this; most accept it but want it to be humane and reforming.

topics.title: Forgiveness
topics.overview: Forgiveness is one of AQA's three 'contrasting beliefs' issues for Theme E. Know Christian and Jewish teaching, how they differ (for example on whether forgiveness needs repentance, and who can forgive), real examples, and how forgiveness fits with justice and punishment.

bullets: **Forgiveness** means showing grace and mercy and pardoning someone for what they have done wrong, letting go of anger and the wish for revenge.

Forgiveness is not the same as excusing the crime or cancelling punishment. Examiners stress that a person can be forgiven by the victim and still be punished by the state, because the court, not the victim, decides the sentence.
Christians believe God forgives sins through Jesus' death and resurrection, so they must forgive others: 'even as Christ forgave you, so you also do' (Colossians 3:13).

In the Lord's Prayer Christians ask God to 'forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors' (Matthew 6:12), and Jesus warned that those who will not forgive will not be forgiven (Matthew 6:14-15).

Jesus told Peter to forgive 'seventy times seven' times (Matthew 18:22; some translations say 'seventy-seven times'), meaning without limit. The parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21-35) shows that people forgiven by God must forgive others.
On the cross Jesus prayed, 'Father, forgive them, for they don't know what they are doing' (Luke 23:34).

Contrasts within Christianity: many Christians say forgiveness should be offered unconditionally; others point to Luke 17:3, 'If he repents, forgive him', and say full forgiveness and reconciliation need the offender to be sorry. Catholics teach that God's forgiveness is received through repentance and the sacrament of reconciliation (confession). Most Christians say forgiveness and punishment can go together.

Examples: Gee Walker forgave the racist killers of her son Anthony in Liverpool in 2005. Maureen Greaves forgave the young men who killed her husband Alan, a church organist, in Sheffield on Christmas Eve 2012. Relatives of victims of the 2015 Charleston church shooting forgave the killer. Others, such as the Anglican priest Julie Nicholson, whose daughter died in the 7 July 2005 London bombings, said they could not forgive, showing how hard it can be.
Forgiveness in Judaism is closely linked to **teshuvah** (repentance): the wrongdoer must feel regret, stop the wrong, confess it, put it right and resolve not to repeat it.

The **Ten Days of Repentance** between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are a time to ask forgiveness. Yom Kippur atones for sins against God, but for sins against people you must first make amends and ask the person you wronged (Mishnah Yoma 8:9).

Maimonides taught that the wrongdoer should ask up to three times, and that a victim who is sincerely asked should forgive 'with a complete heart' and not bear a grudge (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Repentance 2:9-10).

Because only the person harmed can forgive, many Jews believe no one can forgive murder or genocide on behalf of the victims. Holocaust survivor Eva Mozes Kor publicly forgave the Nazis in 1995, saying it freed her from anger; many other survivors and Jewish thinkers disagreed, saying it was not hers to forgive for others. Simon Wiesenthal's book 'The Sunflower' explores this question.
God is merciful: 'Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow' (Isaiah 1:18).

Many humanists value forgiveness because holding on to anger harms the victim's own well-being, and because it can reduce cycles of revenge. The Forgiveness Project, a secular charity, shares stories of victims and offenders.

Others say some crimes are too serious to forgive, or that forgiveness should depend on the offender showing remorse. Humanists generally say forgiveness is a personal choice, never a duty that can be demanded of victims.
**Restorative justice** can lead to forgiveness by bringing victims and offenders together, if both agree.

views.label: Christian
views.text: Forgiveness is a duty without limit because God has forgiven believers, and Jesus showed it on the cross. Forgiveness does not cancel justice or punishment.

views.label: Christian (conditional)
views.text: Forgiveness should be offered, but full forgiveness and reconciliation come when the wrongdoer repents, as Jesus said: if he repents, forgive him.

views.label: Jewish
views.text: Forgiveness is linked to repentance (teshuvah). The wrongdoer must put things right and ask the person harmed directly; that person should then forgive, but no one can forgive on behalf of someone else.

views.label: Humanist
views.text: Forgiveness can help victims heal and break cycles of revenge, but it is a personal choice and never a duty; some may feel certain crimes cannot be forgiven.

Do not say forgiveness and punishment cannot go together. A victim can forgive while the court still punishes.

For 'different beliefs' questions on forgiveness, do not give two Christian points that say the same thing. Contrast unconditional forgiveness with forgiveness that depends on repentance, or with the Jewish view.

topics.title: The death penalty
topics.overview: The death penalty is one of AQA's three 'contrasting beliefs' issues. Know the UK and world context (as of 2026), Christian and Jewish views with denominational differences, and the named ethical arguments: the principle of utility and the sanctity of life, which can each be used on both sides.

bullets: The **death penalty** (capital punishment) is a form of punishment in which a prisoner is put to death for crimes committed.

UK: the last executions were in August 1964. The Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965 suspended hanging for murder, made permanent in 1969 (1973 in Northern Ireland). The death penalty was abolished for all crimes, including treason, in 1998, and the UK has signed international agreements banning it.

Miscarriages of justice: Timothy Evans was hanged in 1950 for murders later linked to John Christie, and pardoned in 1966. Derek Bentley was hanged in 1953 and his conviction was quashed in 1998. These cases helped persuade Parliament to abolish hanging.

World (Amnesty International, report published May 2026): at least 2,707 executions were recorded in 17 countries in 2025, the highest number since 1981, not counting China, which executes thousands in secret. Most were in Iran (at least 2,159) and Saudi Arabia (at least 356). The USA carried out 47 executions in 2025, its highest since 2009. 113 countries have abolished the death penalty for all crimes, and 145 have abolished it in law or in practice.

Israel abolished the death penalty for murder in 1954 and has carried out only one judicial execution (Adolf Eichmann, the Nazi organiser of the Holocaust, in 1962). In March 2026 the Knesset passed a law (62 votes to 48) making death the default sentence for Palestinians convicted in West Bank military courts of deadly attacks. It was challenged in Israel's High Court and criticised by governments including the UK as discriminatory; supporters said it was needed to deter terrorism.

notes.h: Ethical arguments: the principle of utility
bullets: The **principle of utility** says the right action is the one that brings the greatest good (happiness) for the greatest number.

For: executing a murderer may deter others and protects the public permanently, so more people are kept safe and happy. J. S. Mill, a utilitarian, argued in Parliament in 1868 that hanging was a more effective and even more humane deterrent than life imprisonment for the worst murders.

Against: there is little clear evidence that the death penalty deters better than life imprisonment; wrongful executions cause enormous suffering; in the USA it costs more than life imprisonment because of long appeals. Jeremy Bentham, the founder of utilitarianism, came to oppose it, partly because mistakes can never be corrected.

notes.h: Ethical arguments: the sanctity of life
bullets: The **sanctity of life** is the belief that all life is holy because it is created and loved by God, so human beings should not take life.

Against the death penalty: only God has the right to give and take life; 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13); even a murderer is made in God's image and keeps their dignity; execution removes any chance to repent and reform (Ezekiel 33:11).

For the death penalty: some argue from the same principle that because life is so sacred, deliberately taking it deserves the most serious punishment. Genesis 9:6 links the death penalty directly to humans being made in God's image: 'Whoever sheds man's blood, his blood will be shed by man, for God made man in his own image.'

**Catholic**: in 2018 Pope Francis changed the Catechism (paragraph 2267) to teach that the death penalty is 'inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person', and that the Church works for its abolition worldwide. Pope Leo XIV repeated this on 10 October 2026 (World Day Against the Death Penalty), saying justice can be achieved without it. Before 2018 the Catechism allowed it only in cases of absolute necessity, which it said were very rare. Sister Helen Prejean, a Catholic nun, campaigns against it in the USA.

**Anglican**: the bishops of the Lambeth Conference (1988) urged the Church to speak out against all governments that practise capital punishment and to find alternatives that respect 'the divine dignity of every human being'.
**Quakers and Methodists** oppose it because there is 'that of God' in everyone and because of the risk of executing the innocent.

**Some Christians**, especially some evangelicals in the USA, support it for the worst murders, using Genesis 9:6, Exodus 21:23-24 and Romans 13:4 (the state 'doesn't bear the sword in vain'). They argue it is just retribution and that God gave governments this authority.

Christians opposing it also use Jesus' words to those about to stone a woman: 'He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone' (John 8:7), and his teaching to turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:38-39).
The Torah gives the death penalty for murder and some other crimes (Exodus 21:12, Genesis 9:6). So in principle it is part of Jewish law.

But the rabbis made it almost impossible in practice: two witnesses had to have warned the person beforehand, and the court had to give the accused every chance. The Mishnah says a court that executes once in seven years is called 'destructive'; Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah said once in seventy years; and Rabbis Tarfon and Akiva said that if they had sat on the court, no one would ever have been executed. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel replied that this would increase murder (Mishnah Makkot 1:10).
**Orthodox** Jews generally accept that the Torah permits it under a perfect legal system with these safeguards, but many argue modern courts cannot meet them.
**Reform** Jews oppose the death penalty; the Reform movement in the USA has called for its abolition since 1959, stressing the value of life and the risk of error.
Many Jews today oppose its use, while some in Israel support it for terrorism, as the 2026 Knesset vote showed.
Humanists UK and Amnesty International oppose the death penalty in all cases as a violation of the right to life and because of the risk of executing innocent people.

Some non-religious people support it for the worst crimes, such as terrorism or child murder, for retribution, protection or deterrence. Opinion polls in the 2020s suggest a large minority of the British public still support it for some murders.

Points examiners rarely see but reward: a murderer can be forgiven by the victim's family and still be executed, because the state, not the victim, punishes; prisoners in the USA often spend many years on death row, so some have time to reform before execution; and the death penalty is often applied unequally, for example against poor people or minorities.

views.label: Catholic
views.text: Teaches since 2018 that the death penalty is inadmissible because it attacks the inviolability and dignity of the person, and that justice can be achieved without it. Pope Leo XIV repeated this in October 2026.

views.label: Anglican
views.text: Bishops worldwide have urged governments to stop executions and find other ways to punish that respect the divine dignity of every human being while still pursuing justice.

views.label: Quaker
views.text: Opposes the death penalty absolutely, because there is that of God in everyone and an innocent person might be killed. Supports reform and restorative justice instead.

views.label: Christian supporter
views.text: Supports it for the worst murders as just retribution, because Genesis 9:6 says whoever sheds human blood should have their blood shed and Romans 13 gives the state the sword.

views.label: Orthodox Jewish
views.text: The Torah permits capital punishment in principle, but the rabbis surrounded it with so many safeguards that it was almost never used, and many doubt any modern court could meet them.

views.label: Reform Jewish
views.text: Opposes the death penalty outright because of the infinite value of human life and the risk of executing an innocent person.

views.label: Utilitarian
views.text: Judges it by consequences: it is right only if it protects and deters more effectively than other punishments without causing greater suffering, which many say the evidence does not show.

flashcards.q: What is a crime?
flashcards.a: An action that breaks the law and can be punished by the state.

flashcards.q: Name three types of crime by victim.
flashcards.a: Against a person (murder), against property (theft) and against the state (treason).

flashcards.q: What punishments cannot be used in the UK?
flashcards.a: The death penalty and corporal punishment as sentences for crime.

flashcards.q: What are evil intentions?
flashcards.a: Deliberately wanting to cause harm or suffering to someone.

flashcards.q: Give an example of a wrong action that is not illegal.
flashcards.a: Lying or adultery are wrong according to many believers but are not usually crimes.

flashcards.q: What is original sin?
flashcards.a: The Christian belief that humans have a tendency to sin because of Adam and Eve's disobedience.

flashcards.q: What are the yetzer hatov and yetzer hara?
flashcards.a: The Jewish ideas of the good inclination and evil inclination that every person can choose between.

flashcards.q: Which verse shows intentions matter?
flashcards.a: 'Anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart' (Matthew 5:28).

flashcards.q: List AQA's reasons for crime.
flashcards.a: Poverty, upbringing, mental illness, addiction, greed, hate and opposition to an unjust law.

flashcards.q: How can poverty lead to crime?
flashcards.a: People who cannot afford basics may steal to survive.

flashcards.q: How can upbringing lead to crime?
flashcards.a: Children raised around crime may copy it and not learn right from wrong.

flashcards.q: What should religious people say about addiction?
flashcards.a: Addicts need help and treatment, though they remain responsible. Drunkenness is a sin.

flashcards.q: Give an example of breaking an unjust law.
flashcards.a: Rosa Parks refusing to give up her bus seat, or the Suffragettes campaigning for votes.

flashcards.q: What do Christians say about obeying the law?
flashcards.a: Obey governing authorities (Romans 13:1) unless it means disobeying God (Acts 5:29).

flashcards.q: What is tzedakah and how does it relate to crime?
flashcards.a: Jewish duty of charity and justice. Helping the poor reduces the need to steal.

flashcards.q: Which verse links money to evil?
flashcards.a: 'The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil' (1 Timothy 6:10).

flashcards.q: What is a hate crime?
flashcards.a: A crime committed because of prejudice against a person or group.

flashcards.q: Why do Christians oppose hate crime?
flashcards.a: All humans are equal in God's eyes (Galatians 3:28) and Jesus taught love of neighbour.

flashcards.q: Why do Christians and Jews condemn murder?
flashcards.a: 'You shall not murder', the sanctity of life, and humans being made in God's image.

flashcards.q: What must a Jewish thief do?
flashcards.a: Make restitution by paying back the victim, for example Exodus 22:1.

flashcards.q: How should Christians treat prisoners?
flashcards.a: With compassion and respect: 'I was in prison and you came to visit me' (Matthew 25:36).

flashcards.q: What does 'hate the sin, love the sinner' mean?
flashcards.a: Condemn the wrong action but still treat the person with love and hope for change.

flashcards.q: What is restitution?
flashcards.a: Paying back or putting right the harm caused.

flashcards.q: Is theft always judged the same?
flashcards.a: Religious people may sympathise with theft from need, but still say it is wrong.

flashcards.q: Name AQA's three aims of punishment.
flashcards.a: Retribution, deterrence and reformation.

flashcards.q: Define retribution.
flashcards.a: Punishment as payback for a crime, often called 'an eye for an eye'.

flashcards.q: Define deterrence.
flashcards.a: Using punishment to put people off committing crime.

flashcards.q: Define reformation.
flashcards.a: Helping offenders change so that they do not reoffend.

flashcards.q: Which aim do most Christians prefer?
flashcards.a: Reformation, because of Jesus' teaching on forgiveness and love.

flashcards.q: What does 'eye for an eye' really limit?
flashcards.a: It limits punishment to match the crime. Jewish rabbis explain it as compensation.

flashcards.q: What is a weakness of deterrence?
flashcards.a: It may not help offenders change, and some criminals do not think about consequences.

flashcards.q: What is restorative justice?
flashcards.a: Bringing victims and offenders together so harm can be put right.

flashcards.q: What is moral evil?
flashcards.a: Suffering caused by human actions.

flashcards.q: What is natural evil?
flashcards.a: Suffering caused by nature, such as disease or earthquakes.

flashcards.q: What does Romans 5:3-4 say about suffering?
flashcards.a: Suffering produces perseverance, perseverance produces character, and character produces hope.

flashcards.q: How does Judaism see the story of Job?
flashcards.a: As an example of suffering as a test of faith.

flashcards.q: What is tikkun olam?
flashcards.a: The Jewish duty to repair the world.

flashcards.q: Can causing suffering ever be good?
flashcards.a: Some say yes in limited cases, such as fair punishment or healing, if proportionate. Most say it is usually wrong.

flashcards.q: What happened after the Charleston church shooting?
flashcards.a: Relatives of some victims publicly said they forgave the killer.

flashcards.q: What does Genesis 50:20 teach?
flashcards.a: Joseph said that though others meant harm, God used it for good, showing good can come from suffering.

flashcards.q: What is prison for?
flashcards.a: Protecting the public, punishing, deterring and reforming.

flashcards.q: Who was Elizabeth Fry?
flashcards.a: A Quaker who campaigned for better conditions for women prisoners.

flashcards.q: What is corporal punishment?
flashcards.a: Physical punishment such as whipping or caning.

flashcards.q: What do most Christian denominations think of corporal punishment?
flashcards.a: They oppose it because it harms dignity and goes against love.

flashcards.q: What does Jewish law say about lashes?
flashcards.a: The Torah allows up to forty lashes, but it is not used today.

flashcards.q: What is community service?
flashcards.a: Unpaid work in the community given instead of prison for less serious crimes.

flashcards.q: Why do Christians support community service?
flashcards.a: It aims at reformation and repairs harm without the damage of prison.

flashcards.q: What did the Torah stress instead of prison?
flashcards.a: Compensation and restitution.

flashcards.q: Which prayer links forgiveness to being forgiven?
flashcards.a: The Lord's Prayer: 'Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.'

flashcards.q: How often should Christians forgive?
flashcards.a: 'Seventy-seven times', meaning without limit (Matthew 18:22).

flashcards.q: What did Jesus say on the cross?
flashcards.a: 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing' (Luke 23:34).

flashcards.q: What is teshuvah?
flashcards.a: Jewish repentance, returning to God and making amends.

flashcards.q: What are the Ten Days of Repentance?
flashcards.a: The period between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur for seeking forgiveness.

flashcards.q: What must a Jew do after harming another person?
flashcards.a: Ask the person for forgiveness and make amends before Yom Kippur.

flashcards.q: Does forgiveness replace punishment?
flashcards.a: No. Many believers say forgiveness and justice can go together.

flashcards.q: Who was Eva Kor?
flashcards.a: A Holocaust survivor who forgave the Nazis to free herself from anger.

flashcards.q: When was the UK death penalty for murder abolished?
flashcards.a: 1965, and confirmed permanently in 1969.

flashcards.q: Give two religious arguments for the death penalty.
flashcards.a: Genesis 9:6 and 'life for life' support retribution, and Romans 13:4 allows the state to punish.

flashcards.q: Give two religious arguments against.
flashcards.a: Sanctity of life ('You shall not murder') and the loss of any chance to repent or reform.

flashcards.q: What is the principle of utility?
flashcards.a: Choosing the action that brings the most good for the most people.

flashcards.q: Who was Timothy Evans?
flashcards.a: A man hanged in 1950 for murders later linked to John Christie. He was pardoned in 1966.

flashcards.q: What did Pope Francis change in 2018?
flashcards.a: The Catholic Catechism to say the death penalty is inadmissible.

flashcards.q: What is a miscarriage of justice?
flashcards.a: When an innocent person is wrongly punished.

flashcards.q: When did Israel abolish the death penalty for murder?
What did Beruriah teach Rabbi Meir about sinners (Berakhot 10a)?
flashcards.a: To pray that sins would cease, not the sinners: hate the wrongdoing, not the person.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between murder and manslaughter?
flashcards.a: Murder is killing with intent to kill or seriously harm; manslaughter is unlawful killing without that intent. Intention changes how serious the crime is.

flashcards.q: Give an example of a religious moral law that is also a UK law.
flashcards.a: 'You shall not steal' (Exodus 20:15) or 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13).

flashcards.q: How does a utilitarian judge whether an action is good?
flashcards.a: By its consequences: whether it brings the greatest good (happiness) for the greatest number.

flashcards.q: Which verse says evil thoughts come from within the heart?
flashcards.a: Mark 7:21: 'from within, out of the hearts of men, proceed evil thoughts... murders, thefts'.

flashcards.q: What does Proverbs 6:30 say about a hungry thief?
flashcards.a: People don't despise a thief who steals because he is hungry. It shows sympathy, though he must still repay.

flashcards.q: What does 'dina d'malchuta dina' mean?
flashcards.a: 'The law of the land is the law': Jews must obey the laws of the country, unless they require breaking God's commandments.

flashcards.q: Which biblical figures disobeyed an unjust command from Pharaoh?
flashcards.a: The Hebrew midwives, who refused to kill baby boys (Exodus 1:17).

flashcards.q: What did Hillel teach about judging others (Pirkei Avot 2:4)?
flashcards.a: 'Do not judge your fellow until you have reached his place.'

flashcards.q: How does the motive of hate affect a sentence in a UK court?
flashcards.a: It is an aggravating factor, so the sentence can be increased.

flashcards.q: What did Jesus say about paying taxes to Caesar?
flashcards.a: 'Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's' (Mark 12:17): obey the state, but God comes first.

flashcards.q: How many hate crimes did police record in England and Wales in the year to March 2026?
flashcards.a: 146,825, up 7%. Religious hate crimes rose 13% to 11,419, a record (Home Office, October 2026).

flashcards.q: Who is Gee Walker?
flashcards.a: The Christian mother of Anthony Walker, murdered in a racist attack in Liverpool in 2005. She publicly forgave his killers and the Anthony Walker Foundation works against racism.

flashcards.q: What is a whole life order?
flashcards.a: A UK sentence for the very worst murders, meaning the offender will never be released.

flashcards.q: What did Zacchaeus promise after meeting Jesus?
flashcards.a: To give half his possessions to the poor and pay back four times what he had cheated (Luke 19:8): restitution.

flashcards.q: What is the Sycamore Tree programme?
flashcards.a: A victim awareness course run in prisons by the Christian charity Prison Fellowship, based on the story of Zacchaeus.

flashcards.q: How did the rabbis interpret 'eye for an eye' (Bava Kamma 84a)?
flashcards.a: As payment of money compensation for the injury, not physical revenge.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between individual and general deterrence?
flashcards.a: Individual: putting the offender off doing it again. General: putting everyone else off by example.

flashcards.q: Which verse shows God wants the wicked to change rather than die?
flashcards.a: Ezekiel 33:11: 'I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live.'

flashcards.q: How would a utilitarian judge the aims of punishment?
flashcards.a: By results: punishment is justified only if it produces more good than harm, through deterrence, protection or reform.

flashcards.q: What change did the Sentencing Act 2026 make to short prison sentences?
flashcards.a: A presumption that sentences of 12 months or less are suspended (served in the community), partly because short sentences have high reoffending rates.

flashcards.q: Give three situations where some people say causing suffering can be right.
flashcards.a: Fair punishment, self-defence or protecting others, and medical treatment such as surgery (also discipline).

flashcards.q: What conditions do believers usually set for causing suffering?
flashcards.a: A good intention, a greater good, and suffering that is proportionate and never the aim in itself.

flashcards.q: What is the harm principle?
flashcards.a: J. S. Mill's idea that people should be free to act as they wish unless they harm others.

flashcards.q: What does Hebrews 12:11 say about discipline?
flashcards.a: It feels painful at the time but later produces 'the peaceful fruit of righteousness'.

flashcards.q: What is a common criticism of the utilitarian view of causing suffering?
flashcards.a: It could justify punishing an innocent person if that made more people happy, which seems clearly unjust.

flashcards.q: Where in the UK is smacking children banned, and what is the position in England?
flashcards.a: Banned in Scotland (2020) and Wales (2022). As of 2026 England still allows the 'reasonable punishment' defence.

flashcards.q: When did UK courts stop using corporal punishment, and when was it banned in state schools?
flashcards.a: Courts: 1948. State schools: 1987 (all schools by 2003).

flashcards.q: How many hours of unpaid work can a court order?
flashcards.a: Between 40 and 300 hours.

flashcards.q: What did the Sentencing Act 2026 change?
flashcards.a: Short sentences (12 months or less) are presumed to be suspended and served in the community, and many prisoners can be released after a third of their sentence.

flashcards.q: Why did the Torah limit lashes to forty?
flashcards.a: So that the offender would not be degraded or humiliated (Deuteronomy 25:3): it protected human dignity.

flashcards.q: What did Maimonides teach about forgiving someone who asks?
flashcards.a: The wrongdoer should ask up to three times, and the victim should forgive 'with a complete heart' and not bear a grudge.

flashcards.q: Why do many Jews say murder cannot be forgiven by other people?
flashcards.a: Because only the person harmed can forgive, and the victim is dead.

flashcards.q: Who is Maureen Greaves?
flashcards.a: A Christian from Sheffield who forgave the young men who killed her husband Alan, a church organist, on Christmas Eve 2012.

flashcards.q: Which verse links forgiveness to repentance?
flashcards.a: Luke 17:3: 'If your brother sins against you, rebuke him. If he repents, forgive him.'

flashcards.q: Can a person be forgiven and still be punished?
flashcards.a: Yes. The victim can forgive, but the court decides the punishment, so justice can still be done.

flashcards.q: What is the parable of the unforgiving servant about?
flashcards.a: A servant forgiven a huge debt refuses to forgive a small one; it teaches that those forgiven by God must forgive others (Matthew 18:21-35).

flashcards.q: When was the death penalty abolished in the UK for all crimes?
flashcards.a: 1998 (murder: suspended 1965, permanent 1969; last executions 1964).

flashcards.q: How many executions did Amnesty record worldwide in 2025?
flashcards.a: At least 2,707 in 17 countries, the highest since 1981, not counting China (report published May 2026).

flashcards.q: What does Mishnah Makkot 1:10 say about the death penalty?
flashcards.a: A court executing once in seven years is 'destructive'; Rabbis Tarfon and Akiva said under them no one would ever be executed.

flashcards.q: What did Pope Leo XIV say on 10 October 2026?
flashcards.a: That the death penalty is inadmissible because it attacks the inviolability and dignity of the person, and justice can be met without it.

flashcards.q: How can the sanctity of life be used to SUPPORT the death penalty?
flashcards.a: Life is so sacred that deliberately taking it deserves the gravest punishment; Genesis 9:6 links execution to humans being made in God's image.

flashcards.q: Which utilitarian supported the death penalty for the worst murders, and which came to oppose it?
flashcards.a: J. S. Mill supported it in 1868 as a deterrent; Jeremy Bentham came to oppose it because mistakes cannot be corrected.

flashcards.q: What did Israel's Knesset pass in March 2026?
flashcards.a: A law making death the default sentence for Palestinians convicted in West Bank military courts of deadly attacks; it was challenged in court and criticised as discriminatory.

flashcards.q: What did the 1988 Lambeth Conference say about capital punishment?
flashcards.a: It urged the Church to speak out against all governments that use it and to find alternatives that respect the divine dignity of every human being.

quiz.q: Which describes an action that breaks the law?
quiz.why: A crime is an action that breaks the law.

quiz.q: Which punishment is not used in the UK?
quiz.why: The UK abolished the death penalty for murder in 1965.

quiz.q: Which idea does Judaism use to describe good and evil inclinations?
quiz.why: Jews teach that everyone has a good and an evil inclination.

quiz.q: Why do Christians say everyone can do wrong?
options: Because God made some people evil
quiz.why: Christians believe humans have a tendency to sin because of Adam and Eve's disobedience (original sin).

quiz.q: Which is NOT a reason for crime in the AQA specification?
quiz.why: AQA lists poverty, upbringing, mental health problems, addiction, greed, hate and opposition to an unjust law. Retribution is an aim of punishment.

quiz.q: Breaking a law because you think it is morally wrong is:
quiz.why: Examples are Rosa Parks and the Suffragettes.

quiz.q: Which verse might Christians use about obeying authority?
quiz.why: Romans 13:1 says to submit to governing authorities.

quiz.q: Tzedakah helps prevent crime by:
quiz.why: Charity reduces the need to steal.

quiz.q: A crime committed because of prejudice is:
quiz.why: Hate crime targets people because of who they are.

quiz.q: Which verse supports equality and so opposes hate crime?
quiz.why: Galatians 3:28 says all are one in Christ.

quiz.q: A Jewish thief should:
quiz.why: Exodus 22:1 requires paying back.

quiz.q: 'I was in prison and you came to visit me' is from:
quiz.why: It comes from the Sheep and Goats.

quiz.q: Which aim of punishment means taking revenge?
quiz.why: Retribution means punishment as payback.

quiz.q: Which aim aims to put people off committing crime?
quiz.why: Deterrence uses punishment as a warning.

quiz.q: Most Christians prefer which aim?
quiz.why: Reformation fits forgiveness and love.

quiz.q: Rabbis often explain 'eye for an eye' as:
quiz.why: It was interpreted as payment of fair compensation.

quiz.q: Suffering caused by human choices is:
quiz.why: Moral evil comes from human actions.

quiz.q: Romans 5:3-4 suggests that suffering can lead to:
quiz.why: Suffering produces perseverance, character and hope.

quiz.q: The story of Job in Judaism is mostly about:
quiz.why: Job's suffering tests his faith.

quiz.q: Which is an argument that causing suffering may be justified?
quiz.why: Some accept that fair, proportionate punishment causes suffering for a good aim.

quiz.q: Who campaigned for women prisoners' conditions?
quiz.why: Elizabeth Fry was a Quaker prison reformer.

quiz.q: What is corporal punishment?
quiz.why: Corporal punishment causes physical pain.

quiz.q: Community service is mainly linked to which aim?
quiz.why: It helps offenders repair harm and change.

quiz.q: How many lashes does Deuteronomy 25 allow?
quiz.why: The Torah allows up to forty lashes.

quiz.q: 'Seventy-seven times' refers to:
quiz.why: Jesus said to forgive without limit.

quiz.q: Yom Kippur is:
quiz.why: Yom Kippur is the Day of Atonement.

quiz.q: Jewish teshuvah means:
quiz.why: Teshuvah means returning to God through repentance.

quiz.q: Does forgiveness replace punishment?
options: Not always; they can work together
quiz.why: Forgiveness and justice can go side by side.

quiz.q: In which year did the UK abolish the death penalty for murder?
quiz.why: The Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act was passed in 1965.

quiz.q: Which verse is often used to support the death penalty?
quiz.why: Genesis 9:6 says whoever sheds blood by humans shall their blood be shed.

quiz.q: Which Christian argument is used against the death penalty?
quiz.why: Sanctity of life means only God should take life.

quiz.q: The principle of utility is about:
options: The greatest good for most people
quiz.why: It weighs overall happiness or harm.

quiz.q: Which belief would a Jew reject?
options: Everyone has a good and an evil inclination
Humans inherit original sin from Adam
quiz.why: Judaism does not teach original sin; that is a Christian belief.

quiz.q: Two drivers each kill a pedestrian. One did it deliberately, one by accident. Which idea best explains why they are treated differently?
quiz.why: Both actions have the same result, but the intention is different, so one is murder and the other is not.

quiz.q: Which thinker judges actions by their consequences rather than intentions?
quiz.why: Utilitarians judge actions by the happiness or suffering they cause.

quiz.q: Which source best supports breaking a law that goes against God?
quiz.why: Acts 5:29: 'We must obey God rather than men.' Romans 13:1 supports obeying authorities.

quiz.q: A woman steals baby milk because she cannot afford it. Which response best fits mainstream Christian teaching?
options: Stealing is acceptable when you are poor
The theft is wrong but understandable, and the community should help her
She should receive the harshest possible punishment
Only the shop is to blame
quiz.why: Theft is always wrong, but believers show compassion and offer help such as food banks.

quiz.q: Which reason for crime do many believers find hardest to sympathise with?
quiz.why: Greed is selfish and usually chosen, while the others may reduce a person's control or choices.

quiz.q: Which is a TYPE of crime rather than a REASON for crime?
quiz.why: Theft is a type of crime; the others are reasons why people commit crime.

quiz.q: Which source best supports the Jewish idea of restitution for theft?
quiz.why: Exodus 22:1 says a thief must pay back several times what was stolen.

quiz.q: A man attacks someone because of their religion. How does UK law treat the motive?
options: As an aggravating factor that increases the sentence
As a reason to reduce the sentence
quiz.why: Hostility based on religion, race and other protected characteristics makes the sentence harsher.

quiz.q: A judge gives a harsh sentence 'to send a message to anyone thinking of doing the same'. Which aim is this?
quiz.why: Putting others off committing the crime is general deterrence.

quiz.q: Which aim is best supported by Ezekiel 33:11?
quiz.why: God wants the wicked to turn from their ways and live, which is the aim of reformation.

quiz.q: Which philosopher's ideas best support retribution, because offenders deserve punishment?
quiz.why: Kant argued punishment is deserved because of the wrong freely chosen; Bentham and Mill were utilitarians focused on results.

quiz.q: A surgeon causes pain during an operation that saves a patient's life. Which condition makes this acceptable to most believers?
options: The intention is to heal and the pain is proportionate
quiz.why: Most believers accept suffering only when the intention is good and the suffering is proportionate to the good achieved.

quiz.q: Which source is best for arguing that short-term discipline can lead to good?
quiz.why: Hebrews 12:11 says discipline is painful at first but later yields righteousness.

quiz.q: Which is the clearest contrast to most Christians' view of corporal punishment?
options: Quakers who campaign for prison reform
A minority who use Proverbs 13:24 to support physical discipline
Jews who say the Torah limited lashes
Humanists who say it does not work
quiz.why: Most Christians, Jews and humanists oppose it; the minority who quote Proverbs 13:24 support it.

quiz.q: Which crime would most likely be punished with community service?
quiz.why: Community service is used for less serious crimes.

quiz.q: Which belief is most typical of Judaism rather than Christianity?
options: Only the person who was harmed can forgive the wrong
quiz.why: Judaism teaches that the wrongdoer must ask the person harmed; others cannot forgive on their behalf.

quiz.q: A victim's family forgives a murderer, but the court still gives a life sentence. Which statement is correct?
options: This is impossible: forgiveness cancels punishment
The family must now ask for the sentence to be cancelled
Forgiveness and punishment can go together
quiz.why: The court, not the victim, decides punishment; forgiveness is about letting go of hatred and revenge.

quiz.q: Which group's teaching describes the death penalty as 'inadmissible'?
quiz.why: The Catechism was changed in 2018 to say this, and Pope Leo XIV repeated it in 2026.

quiz.q: Which argument uses the principle of utility AGAINST the death penalty?
options: Wrongful executions and lack of deterrent effect cause more harm than good
quiz.why: Utility looks at consequences; the others are religious or retributive arguments.

quiz.q: Which country carried out the most recorded executions in 2025 (excluding China)?
quiz.why: Amnesty recorded at least 2,159 executions in Iran in 2025.

truefalse.s: For Christians, wrong thoughts and intentions can be sinful even if no action follows.
truefalse.why: Jesus taught that lust and anger in the heart are already sinful (Matthew 5:21-28).

truefalse.s: Judaism teaches that people are born sinful because of Adam and Eve.
truefalse.why: Judaism rejects original sin; people have a good and an evil inclination and free will.

truefalse.s: Every sin is also a crime in UK law.
truefalse.why: Some sins, such as lying in most situations or adultery, are not crimes.

truefalse.s: UK law treats deliberate killing more seriously than accidental killing.
truefalse.why: Murder requires intent; manslaughter does not, so intention affects the crime and sentence.

truefalse.s: Christians believe that stealing is acceptable if you are very poor.
truefalse.why: Theft is always wrong, though it may be understandable; examiners did not credit claims that it is 'fine'.

truefalse.s: Many religious people accept breaking an unjust law peacefully as a last resort.
truefalse.why: Examples include Martin Luther King and the midwives in Exodus 1:17; Acts 5:29 supports obeying God first.

truefalse.s: Jewish teaching says Jews should generally obey the law of the country they live in.
truefalse.why: The principle 'dina d'malchuta dina' means the law of the land is the law.

truefalse.s: Hate crime is treated more leniently than other crime in UK courts.
truefalse.why: Hostility based on race, religion and other characteristics is an aggravating factor that increases the sentence.

truefalse.s: Police-recorded religious hate crime in England and Wales reached a record high in the year to March 2026.
truefalse.why: Home Office figures published in October 2026 showed 11,419 religious hate crimes, up 13%.

truefalse.s: Christians believe a murderer can never be forgiven by God.
truefalse.why: Christians believe anyone who truly repents can be forgiven, though they may still face punishment.

truefalse.s: Murder in the UK carries a mandatory life sentence.
truefalse.why: Judges must give a life sentence for murder; the minimum term varies.

truefalse.s: Jewish law focuses on making the thief repay the victim.
truefalse.why: Restitution is central: Exodus 22 sets out repayment, sometimes double or more.

truefalse.s: Hate crime only means crimes based on race.
truefalse.why: It also covers religion, sexual orientation, disability and transgender identity.

truefalse.s: Retribution and deterrence mean the same thing.
truefalse.why: Retribution is payback for the crime; deterrence aims to put people off committing crime.

truefalse.s: Most Christians believe reformation should be an important aim of punishment.
truefalse.why: Jesus taught forgiveness and second chances, and God wants the wicked to turn and live (Ezekiel 33:11).

truefalse.s: Jewish teaching understands 'eye for an eye' as permission to blind the offender.
truefalse.why: The rabbis understood it as fair money compensation (Bava Kamma 84a).

truefalse.s: Restorative justice involves the victim and offender meeting with both sides' agreement.
truefalse.why: It aims to help the offender understand the harm and make amends.

truefalse.s: Utilitarians accept causing suffering if it prevents greater suffering overall.
truefalse.why: The principle of utility judges actions by whether they bring the greatest good for the greatest number.

truefalse.s: Christians believe that because God can bring good out of suffering, it is right to cause suffering.
truefalse.why: Genesis 50:20 shows God brings good from evil, but the brothers' evil intention is still condemned.

truefalse.s: Judaism forbids causing needless suffering even to animals.
truefalse.why: The principle of tza'ar ba'alei chayim forbids cruelty to animals.

truefalse.s: Most religious believers think fair punishment is wrong because it causes suffering.
truefalse.why: Most accept fair, proportionate punishment for justice, protection and reform.

truefalse.s: Smacking children is illegal everywhere in the UK.
truefalse.why: It is banned in Scotland and Wales, but as of 2026 England allows the 'reasonable punishment' defence.

truefalse.s: Corporal punishment and capital punishment mean the same thing.
truefalse.why: Corporal punishment causes physical pain; capital punishment is execution.

truefalse.s: Elizabeth Fry was a Quaker who campaigned for better conditions for women prisoners.
truefalse.why: She worked in Newgate prison in the early 1800s.

truefalse.s: Jewish courts today regularly use flogging.
truefalse.why: Although the Torah allowed up to forty lashes, it is not used today.

truefalse.s: Community service is a form of reparation because offenders give something back to the community.
truefalse.why: Unpaid work repairs harm and benefits the local area.

truefalse.s: In Judaism, Yom Kippur atones for wrongs done to other people without needing to ask them for forgiveness.
truefalse.why: Mishnah Yoma 8:9 says wrongs against people need the person to be appeased first.

truefalse.s: Some Christians believe forgiveness should depend on the wrongdoer repenting.
truefalse.why: They use Luke 17:3; others teach unconditional forgiveness.

truefalse.s: Eva Mozes Kor's forgiveness of the Nazis was accepted by all Jewish survivors.
truefalse.why: Many survivors and Jewish thinkers disagreed, saying she could not forgive on behalf of others.

truefalse.s: Humanists usually see forgiveness as a personal choice rather than a duty.
truefalse.why: They value its benefits but say it cannot be demanded of victims.

truefalse.s: Jewish law in the Torah includes the death penalty for murder.
truefalse.why: Exodus 21:12 and Genesis 9:6 prescribe it, but the rabbis made it almost impossible to carry out.

truefalse.s: All Christians oppose the death penalty.
truefalse.why: Some Christians, especially some evangelicals in the USA, support it using Genesis 9:6 and Romans 13:4.

truefalse.s: A murderer can be forgiven by the victim's family and still be executed.
truefalse.why: Forgiveness is personal; punishment is decided by the state, as examiners pointed out.

truefalse.s: Both the principle of utility and the sanctity of life can be used by both supporters and opponents of the death penalty.
truefalse.why: Utility can stress deterrence or wrongful executions; sanctity of life can stress that only God takes life or that murder deserves the gravest punishment.

truefalse.s: Recorded executions worldwide fell sharply in 2025.
truefalse.why: Amnesty recorded at least 2,707, the highest since 1981 and a 78% rise on 2024.

short.q: Give one example of a religious moral law which some criminals break.
short.a: 'You shall not steal' (accept: 'You shall not murder' or any other relevant commandment).

short.q: Give the meaning of the word evil.
short.a: Extremely wicked and immoral, causing harm or suffering.

short.q: Name the Jewish term for the inclination to do evil.
short.a: Yetzer hara.

short.q: Give one type of crime against property.
short.a: Theft (accept: burglary, vandalism, arson, fraud).

short.q: Give one reason why people commit crime.
short.a: Poverty (accept: upbringing, mental health problems, addiction, greed, hate, opposition to an unjust law).

short.q: Give one example of someone who broke an unjust law.
short.a: Rosa Parks (accept: Martin Luther King; the Hebrew midwives; Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego; the Suffragettes).

short.q: Give one way religious people help prevent crime caused by poverty.
short.a: Running food banks (accept: giving tzedakah or charity; providing shelter; debt advice).

short.q: Give one example of a hate crime.
short.a: Attacking someone because of their religion (accept: racist assault; abuse because of disability or sexuality; damaging a place of worship).

short.q: Give one religious reason why murder is wrong.
short.a: Life is sacred and belongs to God (accept: 'You shall not murder'; humans are made in God's image).

short.q: Name one Christian organisation that works with prisoners.
short.a: Prison Fellowship (accept: prison chaplaincy; Kairos; Street Pastors for crime prevention).

short.q: Give one aim of punishment.
short.a: Retribution (accept: deterrence, reformation, protection, reparation).

short.q: Give the meaning of reformation.
short.a: An aim of punishment which seeks to change a criminal's behaviour for the better.

short.q: Give one way prisons try to reform offenders.
short.a: Education or training courses (accept: therapy, drug rehabilitation, restorative justice, victim awareness courses).

short.q: Give one example of when causing suffering might be seen as good.
short.a: Fair punishment of a criminal (accept: self-defence, surgery or medical treatment, discipline).

short.q: Give the meaning of moral evil.
short.a: Suffering caused by human actions.

short.q: Give one religious teaching against causing suffering.
short.a: Love your neighbour as yourself (accept: 'You shall not murder'; Romans 12:17; tza'ar ba'alei chayim).

short.q: Give one example of corporal punishment.
short.a: Caning (accept: whipping, flogging, smacking, lashes).

short.q: Give one aim of sending a criminal to prison.
short.a: To protect the public (accept: retribution, deterrence, reformation).

short.q: Give one example of community service work.
short.a: Picking up litter (accept: removing graffiti, decorating a community centre, clearing towpaths).

short.q: Give one teaching of Jesus about forgiveness.
short.a: Forgive seventy times seven (accept: the Lord's Prayer; 'Father, forgive them'; the parable of the unforgiving servant).

short.q: Name the Jewish day on which sins against God are forgiven.
short.a: Yom Kippur (the Day of Atonement).

short.q: Give one example of a person who forgave someone who committed a crime against their family.
short.a: Gee Walker (accept: Maureen Greaves; relatives of the Charleston victims; Eva Mozes Kor).

short.q: Give one religious argument against the death penalty.
short.a: Only God can take life (accept: 'You shall not murder'; it removes the chance to repent; John 8:7; risk of killing the innocent).

short.q: Give one argument for the death penalty.
short.a: It deters others (accept: retribution, 'life for life'; protects the public; Genesis 9:6).
