short.q: Give the meaning of the principle of utility.
short.a: The right action is the one that brings the greatest good for the greatest number.

short.q: Name one person wrongly executed in the UK.
short.a: Timothy Evans (accept: Derek Bentley).

exam.q: Explain two similar religious beliefs about forgiveness. In your answer you must refer to one or more religious traditions.
exam.model:
One belief is that Christians should forgive because God forgives them. In the Lord's Prayer Christians ask God to forgive them as they forgive others, so forgiving others is part of being forgiven.
Another similar belief, from Judaism, is that forgiveness is important and linked to repentance. Jews believe a person wronged should forgive someone who is truly sorry, especially in the Ten Days of Repentance before Yom Kippur.
points: Christian: forgive as God forgives; Lord's Prayer; Matthew 18:22
Christian: Jesus on the cross, Luke 23:34
Jewish: teshuvah, Ten Days of Repentance, Yom Kippur
Jewish: forgive if the offender is sincerely sorry

exam.q: Explain two different religious beliefs about the death penalty. In your answer you must refer to one or more religious traditions.
exam.model:
One belief is that some Christians support the death penalty for murder because Genesis 9:6 says whoever sheds human blood, by humans shall their blood be shed. They see it as fair retribution.
A different belief is that Catholics and Quakers oppose it because life is sacred and only God should take life. They also say executed people lose the chance to repent and reform.
points: For: Genesis 9:6, life for life, retribution; Romans 13:4
For: deterrence and protecting society; principle of utility
Against: sanctity of life; 'You shall not murder'; no chance to reform
Against: Catholic Catechism 2018; Quaker view; miscarriages of justice
Jewish: allowed in principle but very hard to apply; most oppose today

exam.q: Explain two different religious beliefs about corporal punishment. In your answer you must refer to one or more religious traditions.
exam.model:
One belief is that most Christians oppose corporal punishment because it harms human dignity and goes against Jesus' teaching to love your neighbour and not to repay evil for evil.
A different belief is that some people use the Bible, such as Proverbs 13:24, to argue that discipline, including physical correction, shows love. Although the Torah allows up to forty lashes, most Jews today do not use this.
points: Against: dignity, love of neighbour, Romans 12:17
Jewish: Torah allows forty lashes, not practised today
Corporal punishment is illegal in the UK as a sentence

exam.q: Explain two different religious beliefs about the aims of punishment. In your answer you must refer to one or more religious traditions.
exam.model:
One belief is that some religious people support retribution because it is fair that wrongdoers suffer for what they did. The Old Testament teaches 'life for life, eye for eye', which they see as justice.
A different belief is that most Christians prefer reformation because Jesus taught forgiveness. They believe offenders should be helped to change, for example through education in prison.
points: Reformation: forgiveness, Romans 12:21, education and therapy
Deterrence: put people off; Jewish view on law being followed

exam.q: Explain two similar religious beliefs about hate crime. In your answer you must refer to one or more religious traditions.
exam.model:
One belief is that Christians oppose hate crime because all people are equal in God's eyes. Galatians 3:28 says all are one in Christ, so attacking someone for who they are is wrong.
Another similar belief is that Jews oppose hate crime because all humans are made in God's image and kindness to others is a key moral principle. Targeting a group for prejudice goes against this.
points: Jewish: God made all humans equal; kindness to others

exam.q: Explain two different religious beliefs about suffering. In your answer you must refer to one or more religious traditions.
exam.model:
One belief is that some Christians see suffering as something that can lead to good. Romans 5:3-4 says suffering produces perseverance, character and hope, so it can strengthen faith.
A different belief from Judaism is that suffering may be a test from God, as in the story of Job, who stayed faithful through terrible suffering.
points: Christian: Romans 5:3-4; Jesus' own suffering; help others
Christian: free will leads to suffering
Jewish: Job, test of faith; hope and faith

exam.q: Explain two reasons why some people commit crime. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
exam.model:
One reason is greed. Some people want more wealth than they need, so they commit theft or fraud. The Bible says 'the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil' (1 Timothy 6:10). This means that greed can lead people to break the law for personal gain, so religious believers would say people should be satisfied with what they have and care about others.
Another reason is poverty. People who cannot afford food or shelter may steal to survive. Jews teach tzedakah, the duty of charity, so the community should help the poor. This means that if a society supports the needy, fewer people will need to turn to crime.
points: Application: believers say be content, share

exam.q: Explain two reasons why intentions matter as well as actions. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
exam.model:
One reason is that Jesus taught that what is in a person's heart matters as much as what they do. He said 'anyone who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery with her in his heart' (Matthew 5:28). This means a person can be guilty of wrongdoing in their thoughts, so Christians try to control their thoughts and not only avoid evil acts.
Another reason is that God knows a person's intentions and will judge them. Jews teach that people have a good inclination and an evil inclination, and must choose between them. This means that if someone intends to do evil, they are choosing wrongly, so repentance must involve changing their intentions.
points: Reason 2: God judges the heart; free choice

exam.q: Explain two reasons why many Christians believe reformation should be the main aim of punishment. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
exam.model:
One reason is that Jesus taught forgiveness. Christians believe offenders can change if they are given a chance. In Romans 12:21 it says 'Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.' This means that responding to crime with help, rather than revenge, is better, so many Christians support education and counselling in prison.
Another reason is that Christians believe everyone is made in God's image and so has dignity. This means punishment should treat offenders with respect and aim to restore them, not just hurt them. Christians support charities such as Prison Fellowship, which helps prisoners rebuild their lives.
points: Reason 2: human dignity, made in God's image

exam.q: Explain two reasons why some Christians support community service as a punishment. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
exam.model:
One reason is that community service allows offenders to reform and make amends. Jesus taught forgiveness and second chances. In Matthew 18:22 he said to forgive 'seventy-seven times', which means Christians believe offenders should be given the chance to put things right and become better people.
Another reason is that it avoids the harm of prison for less serious crimes and shows love for neighbour. Jesus said 'Love your neighbour as yourself' (Matthew 22:39). This means punishment should be fair and help both the victim and community, so unpaid work repairing the neighbourhood is seen as a positive response.
points: Reason 2: love for neighbour; community benefits

exam.q: Explain two reasons why Christians believe in forgiving people who have committed crimes. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
exam.model:
One reason is that Jesus taught Christians to forgive. In the Lord's Prayer, Christians ask God to 'forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors' (Matthew 6:12). This means that if Christians want God's forgiveness they must forgive others, so many forgive criminals even for serious crimes.
Another reason is that Jesus set an example on the cross. He said 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing' (Luke 23:34). This shows that forgiveness is possible even in the worst situations, so Christians try to follow his example, as the relatives of the Charleston shooting victims did.
points: Reason 1: Lord's Prayer; forgive to be forgiven
Application: follow Jesus even in serious cases

exam.q: Explain two reasons why many Christians oppose the death penalty. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
exam.model:
One reason is that Christians believe life is sacred and belongs to God. The commandment 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13) means that killing is wrong. This means that many Christians say the state should not take a life, even a murderer's, so Catholics and Quakers campaign against it.
Another reason is that Christians believe in mercy and a chance to repent. Jesus taught forgiveness and said to the crowd about the woman caught in adultery 'Let any one of you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her' (John 8:7). This means no human is perfect, so executing someone removes any chance of reform and forgiveness.
points: Reason 2: mercy and chance to reform
Application: offenders can repent; miscarriage of justice risk

exam.q: 'The death penalty is never acceptable.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Many Christians agree with this statement. They believe life is sacred, and 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13) means that killing is wrong, even when the state does it. The death penalty also removes the chance for an offender to repent and reform, and Jesus taught mercy and forgiveness. Catholics changed their Catechism in 2018 to say it is inadmissible, and Quakers and the Church of England oppose it. There is also the risk of killing innocent people, as in the case of Timothy Evans, who was hanged in 1950 and later pardoned. This is a strong argument because executions cannot be undone.

However, others disagree. Some Christians and Jews point to Genesis 9:6, 'Whoever sheds human blood, by humans shall their blood be shed', and the Old Testament idea of 'life for life'. They see the death penalty as fair retribution for the worst crimes. Romans 13:4 also suggests rulers can punish wrongdoers with the sword. Supporters also argue it protects society and may deter others, and the principle of utility could be used to say executing a dangerous criminal helps the greatest number of people. This argument is weaker because evidence for deterrence is unclear and because most religious traditions today place mercy and sanctity of life above retribution.

Overall, I think the statement is convincing for most believers. The risk of wrongful execution, the loss of repentance and the value of life are powerful reasons. However, 'never' is a strong word, and a believer who supports retribution for the worst crimes might disagree. Therefore, while I accept that many religious believers have strong reasons to oppose it, the statement is not as certain as it sounds.
for: Sanctity of life; Exodus 20:13; mercy and forgiveness (John 8:7); no chance to reform
Miscarriages of justice (Evans, Bentley); Catholic Catechism 2018; Quaker and Church of England opposition
against: Genesis 9:6; life for life; Romans 13:4; retribution for serious crimes
Deterrence and protection; principle of utility; Israel retains for exceptional crimes
exam.conclusion: Sanctity of life, mercy and the risk of wrongful execution make the statement convincing for most believers, but 'never' is strong for those who support retribution.
points: Developed arguments on both sides with religious teachings

exam.q: 'Prison is the best way to treat criminals.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Some people agree that prison is the best way to treat criminals. It protects the public by keeping dangerous offenders away from society, which fits love of neighbour. It also acts as punishment and deterrence, and Romans 13:4 says authorities have the right to punish wrongdoers. Christians and Jews accept that serious crimes need serious consequences because God is just. Prison can also help reformation if it offers education and training, and Christians are told to visit prisoners (Matthew 25:36). This is a strong argument for serious crimes such as murder or violent attacks.

However, others disagree. Prison can be harmful and may lead to more crime, because prisoners may mix with other criminals and lose jobs and family. Many Christians and Jews prefer reformation and repairing harm, such as community service. Jews link this to tikkun olam, repairing the world, and the Torah stresses compensation rather than imprisonment. Elizabeth Fry, a Quaker, argued prisoners should be treated with dignity and helped to change. This is a strong argument for less serious crimes, where prison may do more harm than good. Non-religious people might also point to the high cost of prison.

Overall, I think the statement is not fully convincing. Prison is necessary for dangerous offenders, but it is not best for every criminal. A punishment should fit the crime and its aims: protection for the dangerous, and reformation for others. So prison is one important tool, but not always the best one, and a fair system should choose the treatment that best fits the crime, the offender and the victim.
for: Protects public; punishment and deterrence; Romans 13:4; justice
Chance for education and reform; Matthew 25:36
against: Prison may increase reoffending and harm families; high cost
Community service, restitution and tikkun olam; Elizabeth Fry; Torah stresses compensation
exam.conclusion: Prison is necessary for dangerous offenders, but different crimes need different treatments, so it is not always the best way.

exam.q: 'Christians should always forgive criminals.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Many Christians agree with this statement. Jesus taught that Christians should forgive without limit, saying 'seventy-seven times' (Matthew 18:22). In the Lord's Prayer Christians ask God to forgive them as they forgive others, and on the cross Jesus said 'Father, forgive them' (Luke 23:34). Christians believe they are forgiven by God, so they should forgive others, even for very serious crimes. The relatives of victims at the Charleston church shooting showed this by forgiving the killer. This is a powerful argument because it follows Jesus' own example and can break cycles of hatred and revenge.

However, others argue that forgiveness is not always straightforward or should not replace justice. Forgiving someone does not mean they should escape punishment, and many Christians believe offenders should show real sorrow before they are forgiven. Some victims find forgiveness extremely difficult, and demanding it could add to their pain. Jews also teach that the person who was wronged is only obliged to forgive when the offender has sincerely apologised and made amends. This argument is strong because it respects victims and the need for justice, and it still allows forgiveness when it is deserved.

Overall, I think the statement is partly convincing. Christians are called to forgive and should always be willing to forgive, because Jesus' teaching is clear. However, forgiveness does not mean ignoring crime or removing punishment, and it can take time. So Christians should aim to forgive, while also supporting justice and the victims of crime, and they should never pressure victims to forgive before they are ready.
for: Matthew 18:22; Lord's Prayer; Luke 23:34; God forgives so Christians must; Charleston example
Forgiveness breaks cycles of hatred; links to reformation
against: Forgiveness is not a replacement for punishment; justice needed
Offender should show repentance; victims may find it difficult; Jewish view that sincere apology is needed
exam.conclusion: Christians are called to be willing to forgive, but forgiveness works with justice and repentance, so 'always' is only partly convincing.

exam.q: 'Reformation is the most important aim of punishment.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Many Christians agree with this statement. Jesus taught forgiveness and love, and Romans 12:21 says 'Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.' Reformation helps offenders change so they stop committing crime, which benefits both offenders and society. Christians believe everyone is made in God's image and can change, and Jews teach repentance (teshuvah) so that offenders can start again. Education, therapy and community work in prison can reduce reoffending. This is a strong argument because if offenders really change, there are fewer future victims.

However, others disagree and argue that retribution or deterrence matter more. The Old Testament teaches 'life for life, eye for eye' (Exodus 21:23-24), which supports fair payback for harm. Romans 13:4 says rulers punish wrongdoers, and deterrence may stop others from offending. Victims and society may feel that justice has not been done if offenders are treated too gently. Also, some criminals do not want to change, so protection of the public must come first. This argument is strong for serious crimes, but retribution can easily turn into revenge, which Jesus rejected.

Overall, I think reformation is the most important aim for most believers, particularly Christians, because it fits teachings on forgiveness and gives offenders hope. But it cannot be the only aim, because justice for victims and protection of the public are also essential. A good system balances all the aims, with reformation as the main goal where possible, because a punishment that changes someone for good helps everyone in the long run.
for: Jesus' teaching on forgiveness; Romans 12:21; made in God's image; Jewish teshuvah
Reduces reoffending; education and therapy; helps society and victims
against: Exodus 21:23-24 retribution; Romans 13:4; justice for victims
Deterrence and protection; some offenders do not change; risk of revenge
exam.conclusion: Reformation fits religious teaching best, but justice and protection are also needed, so the best system balances all aims with reformation as the main goal.

exam.q: 'People should never break the law.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Many religious believers agree that people should usually obey the law. Romans 13:1 says 'Everyone must submit themselves to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except that which God has established.' Laws protect people and keep order, and breaking them can cause harm, as with theft, violence or fraud. Jews teach that following the law is important for justice, and Christians and Jews both condemn crimes such as murder and theft. If everyone chose which laws to follow, society could not function. This is a strong argument because laws protect the vulnerable and avoid chaos.

However, others argue that breaking the law can be right when a law is unjust. Acts 5:29 says 'We must obey God rather than human beings!' and Christians such as Martin Luther King broke unjust laws, using peaceful civil disobedience to challenge segregation. The Suffragettes also broke the law to win votes for women. Jews may break a law to save a life (pikuach nefesh). This argument is strong when the law is clearly unjust, but it is weaker if the protest becomes violent, because Christians must still follow Jesus' command to love their enemies.

Overall, I think the statement is not convincing as an absolute rule. Believers should respect the law because it protects people, but conscience and God's commands can sometimes come first. The best approach is to work to change an unjust law, peacefully, and accept the consequences, as this respects both conscience and the role of authority in keeping society safe and fair.
for: Romans 13:1; laws protect society; crimes such as theft and murder condemned
Obeying law shows justice; Jewish and Christian respect for law
against: Acts 5:29; unjust laws; Martin Luther King and civil disobedience; Suffragettes
Pikuach nefesh may override law; peaceful protest only
exam.conclusion: Believers should usually obey the law, but conscience and God's commands can sometimes come first, so 'never' is too strong when a law is clearly unjust.

exam.q: Explain two different religious beliefs about why people do evil things. In your answer you must refer to one or more religious traditions.
points: Christian: original sin from the Fall; all have sinned (Romans 3:23)
Christian: temptation by Satan, though humans are responsible
Jewish: no original sin; yetzer hara and free will to choose
Non-religious contrast may be credited if relevant: social causes
exam.model:
One belief, held by many Christians, is that people do evil because of original sin. Since Adam and Eve disobeyed God, every human has a tendency to sin, which is why Paul says 'all have sinned' (Romans 3:23).
A different belief is found in Judaism, which rejects original sin. Jews believe everyone has a yetzer hatov (good inclination) and a yetzer hara (evil inclination), so people do evil when they freely choose to follow their evil inclination rather than being born sinful.

exam.q: 'A person's intentions matter more than their actions.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
for: Jesus: sin begins in the heart (Matthew 5:28, Mark 7:21); God judges the heart
Genesis 50:20: the brothers' evil intention is condemned even though good came of it; kavanah in Judaism
UK law: murder versus manslaughter; Kant's good will
against: Judaism stresses deeds: you are judged by what you do; Beruriah: pray sins cease
Victims suffer the same whatever the intention; good intentions can cause harm
Utilitarian: consequences decide right and wrong; James 2:17 faith without works
exam.conclusion: Intentions and actions both matter. Intentions show a person's character and guilt, but actions cause the harm or good that others actually experience, so neither alone is enough.
exam.model:
Some people agree with this statement. Jesus taught that sin starts in the heart: a man who looks at a woman lustfully has already committed adultery in his heart (Matthew 5:28), and 'from within, out of the hearts of men, proceed evil thoughts... murders, thefts' (Mark 7:21). Christians believe God judges the heart, not just outward behaviour. In the story of Joseph, his brothers 'meant evil' (Genesis 50:20), and they are still blamed even though God brought good out of it. UK law agrees that intention matters: a deliberate killing is murder, but an accidental one is not. The philosopher Kant argued that the only thing good without qualification is a good will. This is a strong argument because intentions show what kind of person someone really is.

Others disagree. Judaism places great emphasis on deeds: Jews are judged by keeping the mitzvot, and a person with good intentions who never acts has done no good. Christians can point to James, who says faith without works is dead. Victims also suffer the same harm whatever the intention: a drunk driver who did not mean to kill still leaves a family grieving. A utilitarian would say an action is right or wrong because of its consequences, so a well-meant action that causes great suffering is still wrong. This argument is persuasive because good intentions alone do not feed the hungry or protect the vulnerable.

In conclusion, I think intentions and actions both matter, and it is not right to say one matters more in every case. Intentions decide how guilty or praiseworthy a person is, which is why religions and the law take them seriously. But actions are what change the world for other people. Religious teaching itself joins them together: Jesus said good actions come from a good heart (Matthew 12:35), so the best answer is that they should match.

exam.q: Explain two different religious beliefs about breaking the law to protest against an unjust law. In your answer you must refer to one or more religious traditions.
points: Obey the law: Romans 13:1, authorities are allowed by God; Jewish dina d'malchuta dina
Disobey when law opposes God: Acts 5:29; Exodus 1:17 midwives; Daniel 3
Civil disobedience must be peaceful, open and accept punishment (Martin Luther King)
Two clearly different beliefs, each developed
exam.model:
One belief is that religious people should obey the law even when they disagree with it. Paul taught that everyone must submit to the governing authorities because their authority comes from God (Romans 13:1), so many Christians would campaign legally for change rather than break the law.
A different belief is that it is right to break a law that goes against God's will. When the apostles were ordered to stop preaching, Peter said 'We must obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29), and the Hebrew midwives disobeyed Pharaoh to save babies (Exodus 1:17), so some believers practise peaceful civil disobedience, as Martin Luther King did.

exam.q: Explain two religious beliefs about hate crimes. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
points: Belief 1: all humans are made in God's image and equal
Application: attacking someone for their identity attacks God's creation; churches stand with victims
Belief 2: love of neighbour and the stranger
Source: Leviticus 19:34, 1 John 4:20, or the Good Samaritan
Application: forgiveness and anti-racism work (Gee Walker); Community Security Trust
exam.model:
One belief is that hate crime is wrong because every person is made in the image of God and is equal in his eyes. Paul wrote that 'there is neither Jew nor Greek... for you are all one in Christ Jesus' (Galatians 3:28). This means that attacking someone because of their race or religion treats as worthless someone God values equally, so Christians condemn hate crime and support its victims.
Another belief, from Judaism, is that God commands love for people who are different from you. The Torah says the stranger must be loved 'as yourself; for you lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt' (Leviticus 19:34). This means Jews, who have themselves suffered hate crimes throughout history, should oppose hatred of any group, and many Jewish organisations work against all forms of prejudice.

exam.q: 'Murder is the worst crime.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
for: Sanctity of life: Exodus 20:13, Genesis 9:6; only God gives and takes life
Irreversible: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, destroying one life destroys a world; victim cannot forgive
UK law: mandatory life sentence; humanist: ends the only life a person has
against: Terrorism, genocide or hate crimes may be worse: many victims, aim to terrorise a whole group
Intentions and circumstances differ (te-01): not every killing is equally evil; Jesus: anger and hate begin in the heart (Matthew 5:21-22)
Christian: all sin separates from God (Romans 3:23); murderers can repent (penitent thief)
exam.conclusion: Murder is among the very worst crimes because it permanently destroys a sacred life, but crimes such as terrorism or genocide, which involve murder on a mass scale and hatred of whole groups, are even worse, so murder is not always 'the' worst.
exam.model:
Many people agree with this statement. Christians and Jews believe life is sacred because humans are made in God's image, and the Torah says 'Whoever sheds man's blood, his blood will be shed by man' (Genesis 9:6). 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13) is one of the Ten Commandments. The Mishnah teaches that destroying one life is like destroying a whole world (Sanhedrin 4:5), because the victim's future, and the children they might have had, are lost for ever. Murder cannot be put right: stolen goods can be returned, but a life cannot be restored, and the victim can never forgive. UK law reflects this, as murder is the only crime with a mandatory life sentence. A humanist would agree that ending the only life a person has is the greatest harm. This is a strong argument because no other crime is so final.

However, others argue that some crimes are even worse. Terrorism and genocide involve murdering many people, and hate crimes try to make whole communities live in fear, as the attack on Heaton Park synagogue in 2025 showed. Not all killings are equally evil either: a person who kills in a moment of panic is judged differently from someone who plans a killing for money. Christians also teach that all sin separates people from God, since 'all have sinned' (Romans 3:23), and Jesus said hatred in the heart is already sinful (Matthew 5:21-22). Even a murderer can repent and be forgiven by God, like the thief on the cross. This argument is persuasive because it shows the seriousness of a crime depends on intention and scale, not just the type of crime.

In conclusion, I think murder is one of the very worst crimes because it permanently destroys a life that religious believers see as sacred. However, crimes that involve murder on a larger scale or aim to terrorise whole groups, such as terrorism and genocide, are worse still. So the statement is nearly right, but it would be more accurate to say that murder is among the worst crimes.

exam.q: Explain two religious beliefs about whether it can ever be good to cause suffering. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
points: Belief 1: causing suffering is wrong because of love of neighbour and not repaying evil for evil
Application: rejecting revenge, cruel punishment and violence
Belief 2: suffering can be right if it leads to a greater good, such as fair punishment or discipline
Application: proportionate punishment, surgery, parental discipline
exam.model:
One belief is that causing suffering is wrong because Christians are commanded to love others. Jesus said 'Love your neighbour as yourself' (Matthew 22:39), and Paul wrote 'Repay no one evil for evil' (Romans 12:17). This means Christians should not hurt people, even those who have hurt them, so they reject revenge and cruel punishments.
A different belief is that causing some suffering can be good if it brings about a greater good. The letter to the Hebrews says discipline is painful at the time 'yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness' (Hebrews 12:11). This means that fair punishment, or a parent's sanction, may cause short-term unhappiness but help a person change, so many believers accept it as long as it is proportionate and done out of love.

exam.q: 'It can never be right to cause someone to suffer.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
for: Love of neighbour (Matthew 22:39); Romans 12:17; Jesus healed suffering
Sanctity of life and dignity; Judaism forbids even cruelty to animals; humanist: only one life
Suffering often leads to more harm (cycles of revenge)
against: Punishment causes hardship but serves justice (Romans 13:4); deterrence protects many
Self-defence (Exodus 22:2, Sanhedrin 72a); medical treatment; discipline (Hebrews 12:11)
Utilitarian: right if it prevents greater suffering; Genesis 50:20 good from suffering
exam.conclusion: Causing suffering for its own sake is never right, but causing limited, proportionate suffering with a good intention, such as fair punishment, surgery or defending the innocent, can be right, so 'never' is too strong.
exam.model:
Some people agree with this statement. Jesus commanded his followers to 'love your neighbour as yourself' (Matthew 22:39), and Paul taught 'Repay no one evil for evil' (Romans 12:17). Jesus spent his ministry healing the sick and comforting the suffering, so it seems wrong for Christians to cause pain. Judaism forbids causing needless suffering even to animals, so causing suffering to a person, who is made in God's image, is even more serious. A humanist would agree, because this life is the only one people have, and causing suffering takes away their chance of happiness. This argument is strong because causing suffering often leads to anger, revenge and even more suffering.

However, most religious and non-religious people believe causing some suffering can be right. Punishment causes hardship, but Paul says the state 'doesn't bear the sword in vain' (Romans 13:4), because justice and protecting the public matter. Judaism allows a person to use force against an attacker (Exodus 22:2), and most Christians accept self-defence. A surgeon causes pain to save a life, and parents sometimes discipline children, which Hebrews 12:11 says is painful at first but later produces good. A utilitarian would argue that causing suffering is right if it prevents greater suffering overall, for example deterring crime. This argument is persuasive because refusing ever to cause suffering would mean no punishment, no surgery and no protection for victims. However, the utilitarian view can go too far, for example if it were used to justify punishing an innocent person.

In conclusion, I disagree with the statement. Causing suffering for its own sake, or out of revenge or cruelty, is never right in any of these traditions. But causing limited suffering with a good intention, for a greater good and in proportion to that good, as in fair punishment, medical treatment or defending the innocent, can be right. So 'never' is too strong a word.

exam.q: Explain two different beliefs in contemporary British society about corporal punishment. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
points: Most Christians oppose: human dignity, love, Matthew 26:52, prefer reformation
Minority of Christians support mild physical discipline: Proverbs 13:24; argued against smacking bans
Judaism: Torah allowed limited lashes (Deuteronomy 25:2-3) but not used today; most oppose
Humanist: cruel and ineffective; campaign to end the reasonable punishment defence in England
exam.model:
One belief is that corporal punishment is wrong. Most Christians believe it harms the dignity of a person made in God's image and goes against Jesus' teaching to love others, so they support punishments that reform offenders and many back ending the smacking of children.
A different belief, held by a minority of Christians, is that mild physical discipline can be right. They quote Proverbs 13:24, 'One who spares the rod hates his son', and argue that loving parents should be allowed to smack, which is why some Christian groups have opposed smacking bans.

exam.q: 'Community service is a better punishment than prison.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
for: Reformation and reparation: Ezekiel 33:11; tikkun olam; offender repays community
Avoids prison as a 'school for crime'; short prison sentences have high reoffending; Sentencing Act 2026
Cheaper; keeps families and jobs together; Matthew 25:36 compassion
against: Dangerous offenders must be kept away to protect the public; Romans 13:4
Justice and retribution for serious crimes: Exodus 21:23-24; victims may feel community service is too soft
Prison can also reform through education and chaplaincy (Prison Fellowship)
exam.conclusion: For minor crimes community service is usually better because it reforms and repairs, but it cannot replace prison for serious and dangerous offenders, so it depends on the crime.
exam.model:
Some people agree with this statement. Community service helps offenders reform and give something back, which fits Christian teaching that God wants wrongdoers to 'turn from his way and live' (Ezekiel 33:11) and the Jewish ideas of teshuvah and tikkun olam, repairing the world. Unpaid work such as clearing litter or removing graffiti directly benefits the community that was harmed. Prison, by contrast, can be a 'school for crime': in recent years more than half of adults leaving short prison sentences reoffended within a year, which is one reason the Sentencing Act 2026 presumes that short sentences are served in the community. Community service also lets offenders keep their jobs and families, and costs far less. This is a strong argument for less serious crimes.

However, others argue that prison is sometimes better. Community service is only suitable for minor crimes; dangerous offenders such as violent criminals must be kept away from the public, and Paul says the state 'doesn't bear the sword in vain' (Romans 13:4) to protect people. Many believers also think justice requires that serious crimes receive serious punishment: 'life for life, eye for eye' (Exodus 21:23-24) teaches that punishment should match the crime, and victims may feel community service is too soft. Prison can also reform: chaplains and charities such as Prison Fellowship run education and victim awareness courses, and Jesus told his followers to visit prisoners (Matthew 25:36). This argument is persuasive because protecting the public is a key aim of punishment.

In conclusion, I think community service is better for minor crimes, because it achieves reformation and reparation without the damage prison often causes. But it cannot replace prison for serious or dangerous offenders. So the statement is true in many cases, but which punishment is better depends on the crime and the risk the offender poses.

exam.q: Explain two different beliefs in contemporary British society about forgiveness. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
points: Christian: unconditional, without limit (Matthew 18:22, Luke 23:34); Gee Walker
Christian conditional view: forgive if he repents (Luke 17:3)
Jewish: tied to teshuvah; must ask the person harmed; no one can forgive on behalf of a murdered victim (Mishnah Yoma 8:9)
Humanist: personal choice, not a duty; may be impossible for some crimes
exam.model:
One belief, held by many Christians, is that forgiveness should be given without limit, even if the offender is not sorry. Jesus told Peter to forgive 'seventy times seven' times and forgave those crucifying him, so Christians such as Gee Walker have forgiven people who murdered their loved ones.
A different belief is found in Judaism, where forgiveness is linked to repentance and must be asked for directly. A wrongdoer must put things right and ask the person they harmed before Yom Kippur, and because only the victim can forgive, many Jews believe no one else can forgive a murderer on the dead person's behalf.

exam.q: Explain two different beliefs in contemporary British society about capital punishment. In your answer you should refer to the main religious tradition of Great Britain and one or more other religious traditions.
points: Catholic: inadmissible (Catechism 2267, 2018; Pope Leo XIV 2026); Anglican Lambeth 1988; Quakers
Some Christians: support for worst murders (Genesis 9:6, Romans 13:4)
Orthodox Jewish: permitted in principle but almost never in practice (Mishnah Makkot 1:10); Reform Jewish: opposed
Non-religious: Humanists UK oppose; some support for terrorism or child murder
exam.model:
One belief is that capital punishment is always wrong. The Catholic Church teaches that it is 'inadmissible' because it attacks the dignity of the person, who is made in God's image, and Pope Leo XIV repeated this in 2026, so Catholics campaign for it to be abolished everywhere.
A different belief is held by many Orthodox Jews, who accept that the Torah allows the death penalty for murder in principle (Genesis 9:6) but believe it should almost never be used. The Mishnah says a court that executed once in seven years was 'destructive', so it would need a perfect legal system with strict safeguards.

exam.q: 'The principle of utility shows that the death penalty is wrong.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
for: No clear evidence it deters better than life imprisonment; wrongful executions (Timothy Evans, Derek Bentley) cause huge suffering
Bentham came to oppose it; costs; brutalises society; unequal use
Religious support: sanctity of life (Exodus 20:13), Catholic Catechism 2267, Ezekiel 33:11
against: Utility can support it: J. S. Mill 1868, deterrence and permanent protection of many
Retribution and justice are not about consequences: Genesis 9:6, Exodus 21:23-24, Romans 13:4; Kant
The sanctity of life may be a better basis than utility; Mishnah Makkot 1:10 shows a religious, not utilitarian, reason for caution
exam.conclusion: On the evidence, the principle of utility mostly counts against the death penalty, because deterrence is unproven and mistakes cannot be undone, but utility can point either way, and most religious believers decide the issue on the sanctity of life and human dignity instead.
exam.model:
Some people agree with this statement. The principle of utility says we should choose the action that brings the greatest good for the greatest number. Many argue the death penalty fails this test: there is little clear evidence that it deters murder better than life imprisonment, and wrongful executions cause terrible suffering that can never be undone, as with Timothy Evans, hanged in 1950 and later pardoned. In the USA, long appeals mean it costs more than life imprisonment. Jeremy Bentham, the founder of utilitarianism, came to oppose it for these reasons. Many religious people agree with the conclusion, though for different reasons: the sanctity of life means only God should take life (Exodus 20:13), and God wants the wicked to 'turn from his way and live' (Ezekiel 33:11). This is a strong argument because the facts about deterrence and mistakes are hard to deny.

However, others argue that utility does not show the death penalty is wrong. J. S. Mill, another utilitarian, told Parliament in 1868 that hanging was a stronger deterrent than prison for the worst murders and protected society permanently. If an execution prevented even a few future murders, a utilitarian might support it. Others say utility is the wrong test altogether: justice is about what people deserve, not consequences. Genesis 9:6 says 'Whoever sheds man's blood, his blood will be shed by man, for God made man in his own image', and some Christians believe Romans 13:4 gives the state the right to execute. This argument shows that utility can point both ways depending on the evidence, and that many people judge the issue on other grounds.

In conclusion, I partly agree. On current evidence, the principle of utility mostly counts against the death penalty, because its deterrent effect is unproven and mistakes are permanent. But utility on its own does not settle the question, since it could support execution if the evidence were different. Most religious believers in Britain oppose it mainly because of the sanctity of life and human dignity, which I think is a firmer basis than calculating consequences.
